content.body: Have you ever wondered how to generate all valid combinations of parentheses? This classic problem combines pattern building with careful validation. We'll learn to generate all possible balanced parentheses combinations using a systematic approach.
content.title: Welcome

content.body:
• Apply backtracking to build valid parentheses combinations
• Implement a recursive solution that tracks opening and closing counts
• Explain why we need to validate parentheses as we build them
content.title: What you'll learn

content.body: Imagine you're stacking plates. You can only take a plate from the top (last in, first out). Now think about parentheses: every opening '(' needs a matching closing ')'. How would you ensure you never close more parentheses than you've opened?
content.title: Try it

content.body: For n=2 pairs, valid combinations are: ()(), (()). Try building these step by step. Start with an empty string. When can you add '('? When can you add ')'? Notice you need to track how many '(' you've used versus how many ')' you can still add.
content.title: Explore patterns

content.body: You manually explored building parentheses while keeping track of balance. This trial-and-error approach with constraints is the essence of backtracking - trying options, checking rules, and undoing when needed.
content.title: What you did

content.body: For n=3, there are 5 valid combinations. For n=4, there are 14. Manually finding all combinations becomes tedious and error-prone. We need a systematic way to generate all valid patterns without missing any or creating invalid ones.
content.title: Why it gets hard

content.body: Think of building parentheses like managing a stack of plates. Each '(' is like placing a plate on the stack. Each ')' is like removing a plate. You can't remove a plate if the stack is empty. In code, we'll use recursion to try adding '(' or ')' at each step, tracking how many we have left to use.
content.title: Key idea
content.visualMetaphor: Stack: pile of plates. Queue: people in a line.

content.body: We'll use backtracking with two counters: one for remaining '(' to add, one for remaining ')' to add. We can add '(' if we have any left. We can add ')' only if we have more ')' left than '(' (meaning we have unclosed openings). When both counters reach zero, we have a valid combination.
content.title: The approach

content.body:
1. Start with empty string and n for both opening and closing counts
2. If opening count > 0, add '(' and recurse with reduced opening count
3. If closing count > opening count, add ')' and recurse with reduced closing count
4. When both counts are 0, save the current string
5. Backtrack by removing the last character to try other options
content.title: Steps

steps.title: Create the function skeleton
steps.instruction: Create a function generateParenthesis that takes n as parameter and returns an array of strings.
steps.hint: Start with function declaration and return statement.
steps.expectedOutcome: Function declaration with parameter n returning empty array
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've set up the function structure.
steps.feedbackPartial: Almost there. Make sure you're returning an array.
steps.feedbackWrong: Let's try again. We need a function that takes n and returns an array.

steps.title: Add the backtracking helper
steps.instruction: Inside generateParenthesis, define a helper function backtrack that takes current string, open count, and close count.
steps.hint: The helper will be recursive and modify the result array.
steps.expectedOutcome: Helper function defined inside main function
steps.feedbackCorrect: Perfect! The helper will do the recursive work.
steps.feedbackPartial: Close. Make sure the helper takes three parameters.
steps.feedbackWrong: Remember: backtrack(current, open, close) inside generateParenthesis.

steps.title: Add base case
steps.instruction: In the backtrack helper, add the base case: if open and close are both 0, push current string to result and return.
steps.hint: Check if both counts reached zero.
steps.expectedOutcome: Base case that adds complete combinations to result
steps.feedbackPartial: Almost. Check if open === 0 AND close === 0.
steps.feedbackWrong: When both counts are zero, we have a complete valid combination.

steps.title: Add opening parenthesis condition
steps.instruction: After base case, add condition: if open > 0, call backtrack with '(' added, open-1, close.
steps.hint: We can add '(' as long as we have opening parentheses left.
steps.expectedOutcome: Condition to add opening parenthesis when available
steps.feedbackWrong: We can add '(' whenever we have opening parentheses remaining.

steps.title: Add closing parenthesis condition
steps.instruction: Add the final condition: if close > open, call backtrack with ')' added, open, close-1. Then call backtrack initially with empty string, n, n.
steps.hint: We can add ')' only if we have more closing than opening left (unclosed openings).
steps.expectedOutcome: Complete function with both conditions and initial call
steps.feedbackCorrect: Perfect! You've implemented the full solution.
steps.feedbackPartial: Don't forget to add the initial call: backtrack('', n, n).
steps.feedbackWrong: We need to add ')' when close > open, and start the recursion.

content.body: Excellent! You've implemented the generate parentheses algorithm using backtracking. Remember: the key insight is tracking available opening and closing counts, and only adding ')' when there are unclosed openings. This approach ensures all combinations are valid and complete. The stack-like behavior (last opened, first closed) is managed implicitly through the recursion stack.
